➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.

One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.

Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.

I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"

The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.

But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.

But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...

The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.

That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.

If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

In an interview with IRNA, Brigadier General Ali Balali stressed the full readiness of Iran’s Armed Forces to carry out orders issued by the Commander-in-Chief Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, saying the IRGC Aerospace Force and other branches of the military possess the capabilities required to fulfill their assigned missions and will implement orders without delay.
​
He also said Iran has the necessary capacity to conduct missile operations in new geographical areas, stressing that appropriate measures would be taken if such orders were issued.
​
Describing its sustained ability to respond as a key component of Iran’s defensive capabilities, Balali said the country faces no limitations on the number of missiles, their deployment locations, or available capabilities. He added that Iran’s adversaries face challenges in intercepting Iranian missiles, including the need to acquire advanced systems such as Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD).
​
He also pointed to Iran’s missile cities and defense infrastructure as evidence of the country’s military capabilities, saying that maintaining these capabilities would deter adversaries from taking provocative actions.
​
Emphasizing the role of the people in safeguarding the country’s security and power, Balali described them as the main pillar of the Islamic Republic and the Armed Forces.
​
He added that the Armed Forces have always served the nation by defending Iran’s security and independence, while the people’s participation in the field has reflected their own will and determination.
​
Balali further said the enemy seeks to influence public opinion by spreading contradictory reports and raising issues such as negotiations, the movement of military equipment, and military threats, aiming to create anxiety, division, and uncertainty in society. He urged the public to remain calm, rely on the country’s official positions, and avoid being influenced by enemy propaganda.
​
He also pointed to the adversaries’ failure to achieve their objectives and regional countries’ awareness of the consequences of cooperation with the United States, stressing that Iran’s Armed Forces remain fully prepared and will respond decisively to any hostile action.

There is currently nearly $1.5 trillion in the U.S. stock market that investors don't actually have.

This refers to margin debt — money investors borrow from their brokers to buy even more stocks. Over the past year, the amount of this debt has grown from approximately $1.06 trillion to $1.48 trillion. In other words, more than $400 billion in borrowed money has flowed into the market in less than a year.

When compared to the total money supply in the economy, this figure is now close to its all-time highs. The market saw similarly extreme levels in 2000, ahead of the dot-com crash, and in 2008, before the financial crisis.

But it's important not to jump to overly simplistic conclusions here. A high level of borrowing doesn't necessarily mean the market is about to crash tomorrow. In fact, it's a poor indicator of an exact market peak. The real danger lies elsewhere.

As long as the market keeps rising, leverage accelerates those gains. But when a major sell-off begins, the same mechanism works in reverse. Investors face margin calls, start closing their positions, and their selling pushes the market even lower, triggering more forced selling. What starts as a normal correction can quickly turn into a full-blown avalanche.

And this is what makes the current situation particularly interesting. The market is seeing an unprecedented concentration of capital in a handful of tech companies, record investment in AI, and nearly record levels of buying with borrowed money — all at the same time.

So the question now isn't even whether there's a bubble. What's far more important is what happens when the market actually starts to deflate.

Because the more investors use leverage, the fewer of them will be able to simply sit back and ride out a downturn. At some point, people start selling not because they want to, but because they have no choice.
